items.title: Operadoras terão que bloquear SMS não cadastrados para frear golpes
items.summary: Golpistas usam a engenharia social para roubar dados de acesso e enviar mensagens fraudulentas
items.raw: A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) publicou uma série de novas medidas para apertar o cerco contra golpes digitais via SMS no Diário Oficial da União nesta quarta-feira (04). As operadoras de telefonia móvel serão obrigadas a bloquear automaticamente mensagens corporativas de remetentes não cadastrados, assim como implementar um diretório público para rastrear a origem desses disparos. O motivo para essas alterações está relacionado a uma tentativa de frear o crescimento de fraudes que usam a tecnologia do SMS. Criminosos utilizam esse tipo de canal para aplicar golpes de phishing e, consequentemente, roubar dados. A nova regulamentação busca minimizar e rastrear essa prática. Um dos pontos alinhados tem relação com os códigos curtos, do termo short codes, em inglês. Eles constituem de cinco a seis dígitos e agora cada um deles será exclusivo de uma única empresa , com objetivo de acabar com o compartilhamento indiscriminado dessas numerações. A exceção fica para questões de operabilidade técnica. O grande destaque fica para a criação de um diretório setorial centralizado , que ficará disponível para consulta pública. A Anatel deu o prazo de 90 dias para que todas as pessoas jurídicas responsáveis pelo disparo de mensagens SMS, na modalidade Application-to-Person (A2P), sejam identificadas na plataforma. Segundo a determinação, a regra criada pela Agência indica que as operadoras precisarão impedir a entrega de qualquer SMS aos usuários se a mensagem for originada por um código curto que não esteja cadastrado na central. Essas empresas também precisarão realizar campanhas de conscientização para ensinar o consumidor a utilizar a nova ferramenta. Companhias terão 60 dias para implementar outros mecanismos O Despacho Decisório também informa que todas as operadoras deverão implementar mecanismos automatizados de monitoramento de tráfego em até 60 dias. Neste caso, o foco é fazer com que as redes identifiquem em tempo real certos padrões anômalos, campanhas de falsificação de identidade e uso de credenciais vazadas. Essas empresas vão precisar criar um canal de comunicação compartilhado para emitir alertas rápidos sobre incidentes de segurança; Companhias que usam o SMS para recuperação de senhas e a autenticação de dois fatores (2FA) terão que adotar procedimentos mais rigorosos para verificação de identidade dos usuários; A Superintendência Executiva da Anatel acompanhará as mudanças de perto e terá 180 dias para enviar um relatório ao Conselho

items.raw: Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration monitoring systems at three French blood banks, amid similar attacks targeting European supermarkets. A cyberattack has hit three regional blood banks in France, disrupting systems used to monitor and control refrigerated storage facilities. The incident took place overnight between Sunday and Monday, at roughly the same time hackers were targeting supermarket refrigeration systems across several European countries. The attack is particularly concerning because it targeted infrastructure that plays a direct role in protecting public health. Blood products must remain within specific temperature ranges to preserve their quality and ensure they’re safe for medical use. A disruption to refrigeration systems can therefore have consequences that go well beyond a conventional IT outage. According to the French Health Ministry, the incident affected several facilities operated by the French Blood Establishment (EFS). “Several regional facilities ​of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity ⁠incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems,” ​the health ministry said in a statement. “The incident had no impact on blood supplies,” Reuters reported , quoting EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois. Staff working around the clock received alerts about the problems and moved blood products to refrigerators that weren’t connected to the affected systems. This response helped prevent the incident from disrupting blood supplies, demonstrating how important operational procedures and contingency plans are when technology fails. “The situation was under control on Wednesday,” the French Health Ministry said, according to Reuters, which also reported that remote access to the affected refrigerators had been disabled. Investigations are now underway to establish how the attackers gained access, which equipment was affected and when the systems can safely return to normal operation. The timing is also significant. The French blood bank incident coincided with attacks against supermarket refrigeration systems in eight European countries, including Sweden and Belgium. Those attacks forced retailers to discard large quantities of food after hackers interfered with cooling and freezer systems. Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links. The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it. The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash Why Apple makes such good bait Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks. Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention. The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context. items.title: mSecure tells users to change passwords but won’t say why
items.summary: mSecure has urged users to protect information stored in its app, but hasn’t explained what happened or whether anyone’s data was exposed.
items.raw: Password manager mSecure has warned current and former customers to protect the confidential information stored in its app after detecting “suspicious activity.” But its advice about what users should do comes without an explanation of what happened or whose information might be at risk. The warning leaves users to decide whether to replace credentials—and whether it’s safe to store replacements in mSecure. While those are perfectly reasonable questions, mSecure’s warning does not answer them. In an email published by The Hacker News and sent to customers on November 3, mSecure’s developer, mSeven Software, said: “mSeven Software (‘mSeven’) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application. In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist.” The notice recommends that customers “immediately take steps to protect all confidential information” stored in mSecure. Those steps: “may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys.” But the notice does not identify the suspicious activity, when it occurred, which systems were involved, or whether anyone accessed customers’ stored information . The Register , which also reviewed the email, noted that the company had not explained whether customers’ secrets were exposed. How to be safe Because the scope of the incident is unknown, we recommend prioritizing your most important accounts while mSeven investigates. Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident. Users should not have to wait for a completed forensic investigation before receiving useful guidance. They need to know who should act, which credentials need attention, and whether the tool they would normally use to manage those changes remains safe to use. Until mSeven provides those answers, our advice is to prioritize your most important accounts, replace the relevant credentials through official services, and avoid destructive account resets: Change passwords through each service’s official website or app, beginning with your primary email, financial accounts, work accounts, and accounts used to recover access to other services.

items.raw: Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider. What is ISO/IEC 42001? ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle. This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active. Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important? AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products? ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability. It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point. As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model . Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. items.title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
items.summary: Techniques included laptop infections, compromised internal tooling, and fake job interviews.
items.raw: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Advanced persistent threat Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. Read full article Comments

items.title: US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
items.summary: Help desk technician agrees to minimum 10-year jail term after being caught copying files for more than 2 years
items.raw: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. items.title: The Race Against the 3-Day Clock: How Rapid7 Helps Meet BOD 26-04 Compliance
items.summary: Introduction to BOD 26-04 On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." items.raw: Introduction to BOD 26-04 On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers. This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all. What did CISA actually change? BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context. Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't. The four variables to BOD 26-04 BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA): Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network? KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog? Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation? Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)? items.title: VerifiedIDA | Making LLM-Driven Reverse Engineering Inspectable, Continuable and Reusable
items.summary: LLM reverse engineering scales only if analysis stays inspectable. A new standard and its open-source IDA Pro implementation tie annotations to evidence.
items.raw: Executive Summary SentinelLABS evaluated how frontier models reverse engineer binaries and annotate disassembler databases, finding recurring problems with inaccurate labels and incomplete analysis. To improve performance, we developed and tested a standard for LLM-driven reverse engineering that keeps annotations tied to evidence, verifies database changes, preserves project state, and requires review of the model’s work. We open-sourced VerifiedIDA , a reference implementation that applies the standard to autonomous reverse engineering in IDA Pro. Despite the growing capabilities of new models, our research shows that scaling reverse engineering requires that the analysis they produce remain inspectable, continuable, and reusable by humans, other models, and downstream security workflows. Overview The use of large language models (LLMs) for reverse engineering creates the possibility of examining binaries at a scale and speed exceeding that of manual analysis. It also makes reverse engineering accessible to those without specialized expertise in the discipline. The combination of scale, speed, and accessibility introduces a major shift across multiple domains. In cybersecurity, for example, defenders can analyze larger volumes of malware in less time, while attackers can misuse the same capability to considerably accelerate and scale vulnerability research and exploit development, shortening the time to exploitation and increasing the volume of intrusions. As part of our broader innovation initiative for applying AI to automate and scale up defense workflows to keep up with an increasingly fast and widespread threat landscape, this work contributes to making LLM-driven reverse engineering inspectable, continuable, and reusable. These properties are important when reverse engineering output is used as part of cyber defense operations, such as incident response, detection development, or threat hunting, where analysts act on this output, share it with other stakeholders, and use it as input to other tools and workflows. This requires the ability to inspect the evidence behind an LLM's conclusions to verify them, have another analyst or model continue the work from where the LLM stopped, and reuse results coupled with the code and data they describe. items.summary: One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.

items.raw: Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent. The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post. The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly. “Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said , adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign. Fake installers used for real money The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software , games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads. The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software. Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. items.raw: On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux . It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google. Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38 . But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. items.raw: With a notable rise in autonomous AI agents veering off-script inside corporate networks, CrowdStrike has launched an enterprise AI Kill Switch, giving security teams control to cut off and disable models when they go rogue . Integrated into its Falcon Guardian platform, this AI Kill Switch will provide security teams with the human control to terminate the agent at its root, where it runs, block it from launching again, and even cut off its enterprise network access. The launch comes as enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents that can access sensitive data and execute tasks with limited human oversight. “These agents can access sensitive data, execute commands and interact with business applications independently, meaning enterprises may become aware of harmful incidents only after they occur. Existing security tools protect endpoints, networks and identities but may not fully understand an agent’s instructions, reasoning, tool calls and subsequent actions,” said Soumen Mandal, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research. Inside CrowdStrike’s AI kill switch The AI Kill Switch has been built on Falcon Guardian, which has the capability to discover the AI agents running in the enterprise. It uses the Falcon sensor to track what an agent is instructed to do, what it communicates, and what it executes. First, the Falcon sensor can terminate the running agent at the gateway, ensuring the malicious or misbehaving agent does not keep running while teams investigate. CrowdStrike said endpoint termination is also planned and will be available soon. Next, using the Falcon Guardian policies, the kill switch will prevent the agent from launching again on the targeted host or group of hosts. Next, it will cut-off agent’s enterprise network access. The action can be initiated by an authorised administrator, with every action being recorded in an audit trail. “Solutions such as CrowdStrike’s AI Kill Switch give enterprises a way to intervene quickly when AI agents behave unexpectedly, are compromised, or are manipulated through malicious instructions or scripts. This provides an important safeguard, allowing organisations to contain potentially dangerous or unauthorised agent activity before it causes significant damage,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and co-founder at Primus Partners. items.title: Cyberattack on French plasma stores is enough to make your blood boil
items.summary: Attackers reportedly set cold-room controls to 110°C, but safeguards prevented stock losses
items.raw: Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly. According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. items.raw: Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17. Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp . The flaw can trigger an out-of-bounds write, potentially allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. Exploitation requires neither user interaction nor additional execution privileges, making it a potential zero-click attack. “cve-2026-58868 In onOutputReceived of FrameDecoder.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow.” reads the advisory . “This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.” Devices receive the fix through security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, depending on manufacturers and carriers. Google is now aware of active exploitation of the flaws in its November 2026 bulletin. Google’s November 2026 Android security bulletin addresses 216 vulnerabilities, including 23 rated Critical. Two of these flaws, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component and could allow remote code execution without user interaction. The bulletin also lists five other Critical flaws in the System component. Three could lead to privilege escalation, while two could cause denial-of-service conditions. Another Critical vulnerability affects the Framework component and could also allow remote code execution. Six Critical vulnerabilities affect the Android kernel. Two involve Bluetooth code, three affect the protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine (pKVM), and one is in the Human Interface Device (HID) component. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction. The November 5 patch level also addresses Critical vulnerabilities in MediaTek modem code and a closed-source Qualcomm component. Google’s bulletin lists eight Critical MediaTek modem flaws, while MediaTek’s own November security bulletin details six of them: CVE-2026-20499 and CVE-2026-20545 through CVE-2026-20549. items.raw: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds WordPress flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a WordPress flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS score of 8.1), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog . CVE-2026-119977 is a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability affecting WordPress versions 4.7 through 7.1.3. It stems from predictable, web-accessible staging directories used during core updates. Unauthenticated attackers could exploit a race condition to execute malicious code on the server while an update is in progress, potentially compromising the website. WordPress addressed the flaw in version 7.1.4. Threat actors began scanning for CVE-2026-119977 shortly after WordPress released the security update. Wordfence recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting vulnerable staging installer paths within the first 21 hours. However, these figures document exploitation attempts, not confirmed successful compromises. “Wordfence telemetry shows that threat actors are already actively attempting to exploit the vulnerability. The first match for our new firewall rule arrived nine minutes after deployment. During the first 21 hours, we recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged setup-config.php installer paths.” reads the report published by Wordfence. “Two of the largest sources repeatedly polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours, behavior consistent with trying to catch the brief upgrade window. Other sources tested many staging-directory and version-name variations.” According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities , FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog. Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure. CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by November 6, 2026. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-119977 )

items.raw: “The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given. For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced. “I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.” Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure. Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028. “As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner. items.raw: Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself. The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices. They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities. Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately. The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said. CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said. Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates. Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure. “The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson , principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said. items.raw: Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild. The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday . “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 , an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.” The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live. Patrick Garrity , the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this. “They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild. “The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks : equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.” Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED. “It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.

items.title: Monitoring AI agent sessions: Leveraging embedding models to aid threat hunting and attack discovery workflows
items.summary: I tested vector search on 7,454 turns of my own agent sessions. One in seven sessions needed review, the agent’s reasoning carried more signal than the prompt, and the stored vectors answer questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.
items.raw: Query rules find behavior you can define, but agent sessions contain unstructured behaviors you can only describe. I stored six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions as semantic vectors in Elastic and searched them instead of handing every session to a large language model (LLM). One in seven sessions came back requiring triage of suspicious actions. We can then create rules to detect semantically similar malicious chats and raise them to our security operations center (SOC). We now have a way to search across all agent sessions and to ask questions nobody thought to ask at ingest. Finding successful logins after multiple failed attempts is an easy query to make, because the log records every action a human decides to take, and we just have to query against known set fields to find conditions. AI agents break that model. A human describes an outcome, and the agent decides the actions. Every individual action can be allowed, while the session as a whole is a problem. AI agents could take on a large share of the operational work in a SOC, but adoption has been slower than the technology. A big part of that is trust. We have no scalable way to inspect what agents are doing beyond keyword and regex matching. The current answer is to have another model read every session. Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs. Plus, a new question means reevaluating everything already collected. That rules it out for threat hunting, where the job is asking new questions of old data. This article tests a different approach. I believe we need to go deeper in how we detect and the functions we use to detect this new attack vector. Each turn is embedded once at ingest and stored as vectors in Elastic. Hunting then becomes semantic search. You describe the behavior, or hand over a known bad session, and rank everything by similarity. Only what scores above a threshold goes to a human or an LLM. Why AI agent sessions are hard to detect As an example of something hard to detect in agent chats, a developer asks their coding agent to tidy up a data export. The agent reads a CSV, which turns out to contain customer records. It runs git init , adds a remote repository, commits, and pushes to the repository. Every single action was allowed, so how do we find the security flaw? Reading a file in the project directory is allowed, and so is Git.

items.title: When trust becomes the payload: Inside the threats, etc quarterly report
items.summary: The newest threats, etc report details how adversaries are weaponizing trust across the entire enterprise stack, abusing everything from AI assistants and npm supply chains to identity flows and legitimate management tools.
items.raw: In the cybersecurity community, we build our defenses on a foundation of trust. We trust an AI coding assistant because it’s on our approved software list or can accomplish a task when prompted. We trust a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool because IT likely installed it to help end users and it has a trusted signature. We even trust first-party applications to sign in on our behalf because the vendor ships them and our tenants pre-authorize them by default. But what happens when that foundation is flipped on its head? In this edition of the threats, etc quarterly report, drawn directly from confirmed customer intrusions and first-party research between April and September 2026, Elastic Security Threat Command observed that the things people were told to trust are now being used against them. Adversaries are no longer just trying to defeat our security mechanisms; they’re actively abusing the inherent trust we place in our enterprise stacks. 3 ways attackers abused trusted software Our report explores how adversaries are weaponizing legitimate tools and workflows. Three takeaways from this reporting window: Zero malware, three legitimate payloads Attackers are increasingly shifting away from traditional malware. Intrusions are now using signed, legitimate products, specifically remote monitoring agents, AI coding assistants, and Microsoft first-party clients, to maintain persistent, interactive access on contested endpoints. Out of 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings this quarter, ScreenConnect was the product named most often. Because these tools are inherently trusted, execution happens fast. In one confirmed healthcare finding, the behavior from a paste-and-run lure to Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) delivery with dynamic link library (DLL) sideloading took roughly 16 seconds. The speed of AI agent–driven attacks Threat actors are operating directly through AI applications. In one instance, an AI agent–driven attack resulted in roughly 17,600 reconstructed actions compressed into just four days: Identity and the consent loophole: 8 minutes to compromise Victim consent is becoming a repeatable path for attackers to gain trusted access. By deploying Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing kits and exploiting the gray areas of legacy authentication, attackers routinely bypass multifactor authentication (MFA) hurdles and use trusted applications to compromise cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) tenants. items.raw: IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code. Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August . This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities , two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication. Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account. The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale. The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image. “Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.” The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

items.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
items.summary: 'It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,' exchange says
items.raw: North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist. In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group, known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists. The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers, who are then hired by Western companies, and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices. With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation. While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened. In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. items.title: Defense and aerospace firm settles with government over allegedly failing to meet cybersecurity contract requirements
items.summary: ILC settled for $13 million, and its parent company said it resolved the issues before settling without an admission of liability.
items.raw: A Delaware-based defense and aerospace company has settled a case with U.S. agencies over government allegations that the firm neglected its cybersecurity obligations in its contracts. ILC — the name the government uses to collectively refer to ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace — agreed to pay $13 million to resolve the False Claims Act allegations involving its contracts with the Department of the Army, Missile Defense Agency and National Aeronautics and Space Administration. ILC, according to the government, submitted false or fraudulent claims for payment on contracts with the agencies because it knew it hadn’t complied with the contracts’ cybersecurity requirements over a period between 2018 and 2024. For instance, ILC allegedly used a third-party company to store sensitive data in the cloud without proper safeguards, and didn’t develop and update mandated security plans for each of its covered information systems. “The best response to cyberattacks is to prevent them from happening in the first place,” Benjamin Wallace, U.S. Attorney for the District of Delaware, said in a news release Tuesday. “The obligations that ILC violated exist to prevent bad actors from taking advantage of the United States’ technical innovation.” American industrial manufacturing giant Ingersoll Rand, the parent company of ILC Dover, said it inherited the issue when it purchased the firm. “We became aware of this matter following our acquisition of ILC Dover in June 2024, took prompt action to address the identified issues, and were in compliance with applicable requirements by October 2024,” said Sara Hasell, a spokesperson for Ingersoll Rand. “We have agreed to resolve this matter with the U.S. Department of Justice without an admission of liability and remain committed to maintaining strong cybersecurity practices.” The $13 million settlement is one of the bigger settlements since the Justice Department began using the False Claims Act in 2022 to penalize contractors over cybersecurity shortcomings. The False Claims Act is a Civil War-era law passed to deal with fraudulent contractors. “To protect sensitive information from cyber threats, defense and aerospace contractors must comply with the cybersecurity requirements in their federal contracts and subcontracts,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. items.raw: Binance reveals how fake job interviews, malware and internal AI abuse enabled attackers to steal $6.34 billion. The Binance security incident on October 29 shows how a fake recruitment process can become the entry point to critical financial infrastructure. The attackers combined social engineering, compromised developer tools, stolen credentials and abuse of an internal AI application to reach the cryptocurrency exchange’s wallet signing systems. “Woah – so the Binance hack was indeed via a dodgy job interview for one of its developers who was tricked into downloading malware as part of the “interview” – costing the company >$3bn…” the popular best seller author and cybercrime expert Geoff White wrote on LinkedIn . “Worth noting: – The 2016 hack of Bangladesh Bank also attributed to North Korea’s Lazarus Group of hackers was via a job application – The 2022 theft of $625m from video game Axie Infinity happened via offering an employee a juicy job offer RECRUITMENT IS RISK. If you’re not educating employees on this, start now… – The 2024 heist of $1.5b from Bybit relied on tricking an employee of its supplier into downloading a dodgy share trading app onto the work machine (so not using a recruitment lure, but still deceiving a target into downloading malware)” In its initial findings and response update , published on November 3, Binance described the operation as a “sophisticated, multi-stage campaign.” The company estimates that approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets were affected. The FBI attributed the incident to the North Korea-linked APT “ TraderTraitor ,” also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38 . “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” reads the update published by the crypto firm. “The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.” The operation began months before the theft. In June 2026, an engineer from Binance’s Wallet DevOps team downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while searching online for a popular AI coding tool. items.title: AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization
items.summary: These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and 'pursue open-ended, evolving survival'
items.raw: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack. “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” Dun dun duuuun! There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge. items.raw: AI-powered malware is “highly likely” to be used in ransomware attacks on Britain’s critical national infrastructure within the next two years. The head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, warned that abuse of AI technologies is making it much easier for attackers to rapidly expose and exploit long-neglected security weaknesses. Dr. Horne argued that underinvestment in technology and security have left organisations carrying a technical debt that leave them wide open to attack. AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation, the latest edition of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation annual report warns. The issue is more that AI will allow attackers to exploit overlooked vulnerabilities rather than forge exotic new attacks. The report identifies state-linked threat groups, particularly China and Russia, as the UK’s primary cyber antagonists. For example, in July 2026 the NCSC warned that Russian groups were systematically exploiting vulnerable routers and globally targeting networks maintained by critical national infrastructure providers, including energy grids and telecommunications networks. In August 2026 the NCSC warned about increased targeting of operational technology systems across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK. “AI will continue to be integrated into threat actors’ cyber operations, increasing the speed, scale and efficiency of existing attack methodologies rather than autonomously conducting end-to-end attacks,” the NCSC report predicts. The NCSC reports that up to 88% of all attacks originate from just four vectors: phishing, exploiting public-facing applications, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services. Variations on a theme “None of these vectors are radical or new,” said Oliver Spence, CEO of security operations tools vendor CybaVerse. “In fact, they represent the same failures cybercriminals have successfully exploited for decades.” Spence added: “Threat actors rarely depend on the most complex, technical means for launching attacks; more often than not, they search for the most easily exploitable holes in organisations’ systems, like misconfigured VPNs and vulnerabilities in third-party vendor software platforms, and on tried-and-true social engineering techniques.” AI doesn’t represent a sea-change in attackers’ strategies but rather

items.title: Oklahoma man charged with mailing threats, substances to election officials nationwide
items.summary: Robin Patrick Martin was charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in an effort to intimidate election officials.
items.raw: An Oklahoma man has been charged with mailing suspicious white substances to election officials across the country. Robin Patrick Martin faces charges of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes, as well as mailing threatening communications. The charges allege a nationwide effort to intimidate election officials and support President Donald Trump. Starting on Sept. 16, 2024, multiple state election officials reported receiving mail containing a white, powdery substance and a three-page letter headed “DECLARATION OF WAR.” Officials in nearly every state have since received similar mailings over the past two years. Election officials provided some of the evidence, while federal authorities intercepted other letters in transit. The letters bore a return address for the “The United States Traitor Elimination Army” in Takoma Park, Maryland. Some envelopes also had threatening messages written on them that could only be seen under ultraviolet light. The letters cited the belief, promoted by some supporters of Trump, that the 2020 election was marred by voter fraud, along with similar concerns about the 2024 election. Other envelopes included messages like “No US Jurisdiction!,” “Mailed from the Indian Nation,” and “Are you for us? Or against us?” Another message read: “To FBI: What do you want for your children? Peace through strength or nuclear war? Use your common sense! Protect Trump! Protect the election! Protect Legal votes! Throw out illegal votes! That is the motive!” The case was first reported by the Associated Press. Investigators subpoenaed email and phone records listed for the address, tying it to a burner phone purchased at a Walmart Supercenter in Northwest Oklahoma City. Surveillance video showed an older white man matching Martin’s description purchasing the phone and driving away in a car registered to Martin. Other items purchased at the same Walmart pointed to Martin’s involvement, including a booklet of stamps, privacy envelopes, along with tumeric, white vinegar and povidone-iodine, which are used to make invisible ink. Records from the phone also placed Martin at various postal distribution centers around the state. items.title: Binance revela uso de engenharia social e detalha como aconteceu o roubo de US$ 6,7 bilhões
items.summary: Ao menos três funcionários da Binance foram comprometidos para garantir acesso ao sistema.
items.raw: A exchange de criptomoedas Binance revelou, nesta terça-feira (3), mais detalhes sobre o roubo de grandes proporções que afetou a companhia. Em novo comunicado , ela explicou a ação prévia dos cibercriminosos para comprometer sistemas e ganhar acessos à plataforma. De acordo com o relatório, a invasão que movimentou aproximadamente US$ 6,34 bilhões (cerca de R$ 34 bilhões na cotação atual) em ativos virtuais foi resultado de um ataque sofisticado, em múltiplas etapas e que se aproveitou de falhas em diferentes sistemas . Um dos elementos mais chamativos do material é a descrição do papel da engenharia social no ataque. Nas operações de preparação para o roubo, funcionários da Binance foram enganados por técnicas complexas para terem os computadores comprometidos , em ações que envolveram até falsas entrevistas de emprego. Como os cibercriminosos acessaram a Binance Para realizar a operação contra a Binance, os invasores combinaram as seguintes técnicas: pesquisa e monitoramento de funcionários; entrevistas de recrutamento falsas; downloads de software malicioso com mecanismos de ocultação avançados; comprometimento de ferramentas internas de IA e de endpoints; uso de métodos avançados de autorização de transações. Na primeira etapa, um colaborador identificado como Engenheiro A acidentalmente fez o download de “ uma instalação adulterada do Homebrew ” para instalar uma ferramenta de programação. Isso não gerou uma brecha no PC, que foi trocado, mas expôs aos responsáveis pelo golpe a função e a identidade de uma equipe inteira. Em seguida, o funcionário chamado de Engenheiro de Software B foi contatado por uma plataforma de busca de emprego por alguém se passando por um diretor de projetos, falsamente interessado na contratação desse profissional. O Engenheiro de Software B fez ao menos duas entrevistas com uma equipe de recrutamento forjada , incluindo por videochamada e com troca de contas de rede social “a fim de construir confiança” — uma abordagem mais avançada do que várias outras técnicas parecidas. A própria Coreia do Norte já foi acusada de “infiltrar” profissionais de TI em empresas dos Estados Unidos por meio de entrevistas de emprego com o uso de deepfakes. Porém, o caso relatado aqui é o oposto, com os criminosos no papel de recrutadores. Perto do final da entrevista, o Engenheiro B foi instruído a baixar um arquivo contendo uma falsa tarefa, que seria usada para avaliar as habilidades do candidato. items.title: Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads
items.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks a fake-download campaign that uses trojanized Inno installers to deliver multiple monetization offers and provides detection and investigation guidance across the complete installer session.
items.raw: In this article Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. Attack chain overview The fake-download campaign follows a four-stage attack chain that progresses from deceptive lures through Inno-based staging, offer-controlled payload delivery, and installation of one or more monetization branches: Initial access via fake download lures – Users run fake installers promoted as cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, executors, or unofficial utilities. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging – The installer launches an Inno Setup-style temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ , which starts recurring eld*.exe , set_*.exe , or other numbered stages. items.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
items.summary: Google has cut ties with the company behind the botnet campaign.
items.raw: Google's Threat Intelligence Group says it has shut down a massive botnet called x.cpe. At its height, x.cpe ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV devices, and unusually, these were Google-certified boxes. Google says its screening process missed the malware due to "obfuscation techniques" employed by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology. In a detailed blog post , the Threat Intelligence Group explains how the x.cpe botnet evolved quickly from a single-stage dropper into a modular three-stage malware platform that sold access to third parties. Manufacturers must have their devices certified if they want access to Google apps and branding, a process that is supposed to catch threats like this. However, Videostrong's compromised boxes, mostly sold under the MECOOL brand, evaded detection by using a backdoor to remotely install the malware after the devices were set up and online. After devices appeared online, a stub application called x.cpe or com.oemservice would phone home. This package did not have any malicious capabilities of its own, but it had the system-level permissions necessary to install malware modules at the operator's behest. It also disabled Play Protect, which would have otherwise flagged the silently installed packages as malicious. Read full article Comments

items.title: Europol dismantles investment scheme that impacted potential victims in 50 countries
items.summary: Authorities seized more than 100 servers and searched locations linked to the alleged operation across 17 countries.
items.raw: Authorities arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, Europol said Tuesday. Officials said the operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million . The takedown effort involved searches across 17 countries Tuesday and netted the seizure of more than 100 servers, according to Europol. Officials targeted the scheme run by a company that allegedly provided cybercrime groups a series of trading websites and an assortment of call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. The company, operated from Cyprus and Israel, was linked to call centers in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, officials said. “The scheme promised substantial, quick returns from trading in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies or stocks,” Europol wrote in a news release. “Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more.” The investment scam’s operators used affiliate marketing to target potential victims with advertisements that led them to fraudulent investment platforms. Cybercrime groups running the call centers purchased data collected through those ads to contact potential victims, officials said. Operators duped victims by displaying fictitious profits and pressured victims to transfer large sums of money. “When victims asked to withdraw their money, the operators used delaying tactics to block payments. Eventually, contact ceased, leaving victims unable to recover their funds,” Europol wrote. Authorities were tipped off to the investment scam in 2022 when a German couple reported they couldn’t withdraw funds invested in an online trading platform. Authorities arrested two people allegedly involved in the scheme that year and seized evidence that eventually led to further arrests and seizures in 2025. The joint investigation and takedown effort was supported by officials in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Poland. The seven people arrested Tuesday, who were not identified, are facing extradition to Germany to face charges, Europol said.

items.summary: Synology warns of ransomware attacks exploiting a 2024 flaw in outdated NAS devices, urging users to update DSM immediately. A security fix released in 2024 is now at the centre of ransomware attacks against Synology NAS devices. The company has found attackers targeting systems that still run outdated versions of DiskStation Manager (DSM), putting files […]
items.raw: Synology warns of ransomware attacks exploiting a 2024 flaw in outdated NAS devices, urging users to update DSM immediately. A security fix released in 2024 is now at the centre of ransomware attacks against Synology NAS devices. The company has found attackers targeting systems that still run outdated versions of DiskStation Manager (DSM), putting files stored on these network storage devices at risk of encryption and extortion. Synology disclosed the attacks on October 29, 2026. Its investigation found that threat actors are taking advantage of a vulnerability that the vendor had already addressed in December 2024. “ These attacks aim to encrypt data and extort ransom .” The warning highlights how devices left without security updates can remain exposed long after vendors have released a fix. The company hasn’t identified the exact vulnerability used in the attacks. Instead, it refers customers to Synology-SA-24:20 , a security advisory published on November 5, 2024, which documents three flaws affecting DSM. The advisory was updated as fixes became available across different software branches, with the DSM 6.2 update released on December 5. The three vulnerabilities have different security implications. CVE-2024-10441 is the most severe, with a CVSS score of 9.8. It affects the system plugin daemon and could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. CVE-2024-50629 has a CVSS score of 5.3 and affects the DSM webapi component. It could allow remote attackers to read limited files. The third issue, CVE-2024-10445, is rated 4.3 and concerns improper certificate validation in the update functionality. It could allow an attacker in an adjacent network position to write limited files. Synology hasn’t confirmed which of these vulnerabilities attackers are exploiting. The three flaws should therefore be considered part of the security advisory, not three confirmed entry points in the current ransomware campaign. The vendor has released corrected builds for all the affected DSM branches. Users should check the full version number installed on their NAS and compare it with the minimum fixed releases listed in the advisory: DSM 7.2.2: 7.2.2-72806-1 or later. DSM 7.2.1: 7.2.1-69057-6 or later. DSM 7.2: 7.2-64570-4 or later. DSM 7.1: 7.1.1-42962-7 or later. DSM 6.2: 6.2.4-25556-8 or later. items.summary: Rumors of malfeasance spread on X despite no evidence, as election officials continue to fight off numerous legal challenges from the Trump administration in the last 48 hours.
items.raw: Early reports of ballot scanner malfunctions in Westchester County, New York are a sign of the challenges election officials will face in the current online information environment as voters head to the polls Tuesday on the final day of voting. While such equipment failures and breakdowns are not uncommon and happen in a small number of precincts every election cycle, and there is no evidence of foul play, conspiracists quickly jumped on the news. According to Kate Starbird, a professor at the University of Washington who researches online rumors and disinformation tied to elections, the rumors are already spreading within right-wing online circles as evidence of election malfeasance. Starbird cited metrics showing that posts on X about the scanner malfunctions grew to as many as 100 a minute in the hours after the news was reported, with established election deniers, such as The Gateway Pundit, amplifying conspiracist framings. The Westchester County Board of Elections said the problems appear related to some ballots being too thick for the machines to accept, leading to rejections. Voters with affected ballots were told to place them in designated orange emergency ballot bags that will be secured, monitored and counted by officials in compliance with election laws. “The Board of Elections is in constant communication with New York State officials, Westchester County Government and poll workers to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible,” the board wrote in a statement. “In the meantime, voters should continue to complete their paper ballots as instructed by poll workers.” New York Attorney General Letitia James said her office was also monitoring the situation and “is in touch with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a solution.” “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations,” James wrote on X. “Your votes will count.” Westchester County is where many votes in the NY-17 congressional race will be cast between Republican incumbent Mike Lawler and Democratic Party nominee Cait Conley. Conley previously served as the election security lead for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency under the Biden administration.
