items.title: Password manager mSecure tells users to change passwords, won't say why
items.summary: Customers left wondering what's been compromised after vendor advises resetting passwords, 2FA and passkeys
items.raw: Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register, US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously. "Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys." For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace. The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers. "Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised." Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved. "I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked. A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself. items.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
items.summary: UEFI bootkit BlackX exploits Microsoft's lack of clarity around Secure Boot protections.
items.raw: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational. Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim? UEFI bootkit refresher Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface , UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS. Read full article Comments

items.title: CrowdStrike moves to acquire Fiddler and Dreadnode, adding AI observability and testing to its security platform
items.summary: CrowdStrike is extending its platform to watch, test and explain autonomous AI agents, as enterprises face behavior-based risks that conventional security tools cannot catch.
items.raw: CrowdStrike announced Monday it has signed agreements to acquire two artificial intelligence security companies, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode, in deals announced at its Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona. CrowdStrike did not disclose what it paid for the companies. A report in the Wall Street Journal listed the price for Fiddler at $400 million, and Dreadnode at $95 million. Fiddler, which specializes in AI agent observability and explainability, will become Falcon Observe on the company’s Falcon platform. Dreadnode builds automated security testing for AI systems, checking models and agents for weaknesses before deployment. The acquisitions address a gap that has widened as companies adopt AI agents: the software can hold valid credentials and approved tools yet still make bad decisions, ignore instructions or claim work it never completed. Traditional security testing, built for code that behaves predictably, does not reach the model layer or the agent’s reasoning process. Fiddler’s technology works after deployment. It evaluates agents before they reach production, traces decisions and reasoning across agent systems, flags drifting behavior and made-up answers, and creates records that can be used in audits. It works with common agent frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock and Google ADK. “When a regulator or your board asks what an agent did, saying ‘the model did it’ is not an answer,” said George Kurtz, CrowdStrike’s chief executive and founder, describing Fiddler as “the flight recorder for every agent.” Dreadnode works earlier in the process. Its platform runs more than 100 known attack methods, including jailbreaks and prompt injection, against models and agent systems. It ranks problems by severity and maps them to widely used security standards, such as the OWASP Top 10 for large language models and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Dreadnode Chief Executive Brad Palm said his company was built on the idea that “the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers.” The announcements come alongside new Falcon Guardian capabilities that protect agents while they run. In a separate announcement, Kurtz introduced what the company calls the AI Kill Switch, a control that lets humans stop any AI agent. items.raw: Overview Multiple vulnerabilities have been identified in the Android application, BaseChat – Audio Dating App, version 9.8.1, which ultimately compromise the privacy of users’ personal data and activity. Description BaseChat is an online dating platform built in Flutter and targeted toward users over 18. It facilitates anonymous, voice-first interaction between users. Three distinct vulnerabilities have been identified within the shipped Android application. VU#124705.1: The application fails open when validating TLS server certificates for connections to its backend API host. The application allows any self-signed certificate to bypass standard TLS security checks. VU#124705.2: Paid user accounts are mapped to a third-party RevenueCat subscriber database using raw MSISDNs (phone numbers), which are a guessable public identifier. Because the RevenueCat Software Development Kit (SDK) includes a public API key within the application’s Android Package Kit (APK), an attacker can query the RevenueCat’s API using predictable identifiers to retrieve individual user metadata. VU#124705.3: The application writes Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to Android system logs in its production build. During voice calls, the application logs the remote party’s MSISDN through unstripped debug statements, which allows an attacker to recovery phone numbers of callers who are intended to remain anonymous. Impact Impacts of successful exploitation vary by vulnerability. VU#124705.1: A network-positioned attacker can intercept and modify API communication, potentially leading to account takeover via session credential theft. VU#124705.2: An attacker can locate the public RevenueCat SDK key and query the RevenueCat API using arbitrary phone numbers to retrieve associated user metadata, including activity and purchase history. VU#124705.3: The personal data, or PII, of other users, intended to be anonymous, can be accessed through local system logs. The application’s backend sending other users’ MSISDNs to the client in any capacity presents a privacy violation. These vulnerabilities have been confirmed against Basechat – Audio Dating App, Android version 9.8.1. Solution Unfortunately, Mobile Trading GmbH, the owners of BaseChat, could not be reached to coordinate this vulnerability. items.title: Defrost and Disrupt | An Assessment of Europe’s Refrigeration Attacks
items.summary: Store fridges and freezers warmed overnight in six countries on November 2-3. Russian-aligned groups are credible suspects, but attribution remains open.
items.raw: Executive Summary On November 2 and 3, supermarket chains in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia reported overnight disruption to store refrigeration systems. The incidents came three weeks after attacks on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Attacks on refrigeration systems predate the 2026 incidents, including attacks on Russian supermarkets and Israeli stores documented by Danfoss in 2022, and a 2024 attack on a Los Angeles meat processor that the DOJ attributed to CARR. Reporting and official statements suggest attackers changed temperature and defrost settings through the systems’ own management interfaces. ANSSI’s assessment of the French cases at the time pointed to internet-exposed administration interfaces and weak passwords. Russian-aligned groups including CARR, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest have a documented record of disrupting operational technology and have claimed refrigeration intrusions, making them a credible line of investigation. However, available evidence does not yet establish who is responsible for the European incidents. Freezer failures at U.S. military commissaries in August predate the French attacks. U.S. officials reportedly suspect Iran-linked actors in those cases, an assessment that is provisional and does not concern Europe. Further incidents are likely wherever the same access conditions persist. Copied techniques and opportunistic claims may make unrelated activity look like a single campaign before investigators establish whether one exists. Overview and Chronology Reporting on the recent spate of incidents affecting store refrigeration systems in Europe has moved quickly, at times conflating them with older attacks, hacktivist claims and government allegations about Russian and Iranian actors. The chronology below separates incidents from claims and from assessments. When reviewed in order, it shows similar incidents recurring across countries and months but does not establish that these various incidents belong to a single campaign. 2022 - Danfoss documented attacks targeting 16 Russian supermarkets and affecting 40 Israeli stores. According to the vendor, the affected Israeli installations lacked appropriate firewall or VPN protection. November 2024 - A Los Angeles meat-processing facility suffered an attack that, according to later U.S. Justice Department allegations, spoiled meat and caused an ammonia leak. The DOJ attributed that incident to CyberArmyofRussia_Rebo

items.summary: Videostrong planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android set-top boxes and sold criminals access to the resulting botnet.

The takedown disrupted the botnet, but the backdoor remains in infected boxes’ firmware. Suspect your box? Disconnect it and ask the seller about a fix or replacement. Most malware needs you to click something. This one came in the box. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says it has high confidence that Android device maker Videostrong Technology built and ran the XCPE backdoor for financial gain. Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates, who loaded their own malware modules onto the boxes. GTIG found that the backdoor, called x.cpe (or com.oemservice in some builds), sits in the firmware with system-level privileges. If someone uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition when the device reboots. It could also switch off Google Play Protect app verification, allowing it to install more software without asking. Google says Videostrong got past its compatibility and security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. This allowed the devices to remain part of the residential proxy network. Residential proxy networks rent out ordinary home IP addresses to customers. That makes their traffic appear to come from a legitimate consumer connection rather than a data center. This can help cybercriminals evade IP-based fraud controls and reputation systems. items.title: Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles
items.summary: Key Points Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles Check Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. Besides an open Cobalt Strike server, whose logs showed the actor compromising various private computers of Chinese speaking individuals, other tools from the toolkit of […]
items.raw: Key Points Check Point Research analyzed the Haiou jailbreak bundle, a prompt package targeting OpenAI Codex. Such jailbreaks are designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. The analyzed bundle can be classified as prompt adware . It installs security-focused Skills and modifies Codex’ configuration files so that advertisements for the jailbreak’s author’s website are injected into subsequent agent responses. The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider. The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service. We observed the jailbreak being used by a cybercrime actor, alongside Cobalt Strike, the VulnClaw agent and the Ladon framework. While this does not imply that the package was designed for cybercrime, it shows that these dual-use toolkits are actively used by threat actors. Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles Check Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. Besides an open Cobalt Strike server, whose logs showed the actor compromising various private computers of Chinese speaking individuals, other tools from the toolkit of this actor were deployed on the same webserver: The Ladon framework (a network scanner popular in Chinese speaking communities), the VulnClaw agent (a penetration testing agent, again popular in Chinese speaking communities) and a Chinese jailbreak bundle for Codex called Haiou . While threat actors using AI to augment their hacking operations has become a common sight, the jailbreak bundle caught our attention. Jailbreaks are custom prompts, designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. As frontier models employ more and more guardrails for (offensive) security related tasks and are also hardened against adversarial prompts such as jailbreaks, new jailbreak bundles offer one way for users to enable them to continue to use these models for hacking. Of course, while alternatives like getting approved for cybersecurity use through the provider’s program or using uncensored or self-hosted models exist, jailbreaks are a viable and comparatively simple method. Common jailbreak methods are role-playing or reframing requests into benign context

items.title: Britain on notice: AI-powered ransomware attacks to arrive by 2028
items.summary: Cyber agency warns critical infrastructure is a likely target as chief urges bosses to stop doing 'tech on the cheap'
items.raw: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg, Microsoft 365, and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs, the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. items.raw: The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure. Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations. “That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest,” Microsoft Security researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam wrote in a blog post detailing the findings. They were referring to the distance between how fast flaws are exploited and how slowly critical systems are patched. Patching measured in weeks and months Microsoft drew its patching figures from 2026 data in its Security Exposure Management product. The median vulnerability is fixed in about two weeks on Windows workstations but takes more than a month on Windows Server, according to the post. The delay stretches beyond 10 weeks on Linux servers and for applications running on macOS, and past a year on network appliances . Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer, said the findings reflect what he sees across enterprise environments. In those environments, change approvals, application dependencies, maintenance windows, and legacy infrastructure routinely hold up fixes. “Network appliances are particularly difficult because firmware upgrades can affect critical business operations,” Dubey said. “In many cases, the challenge is not identifying vulnerabilities, but getting the right teams to remediate them without disrupting business services.” Exploitation measured in days Exploitation runs on a far shorter clock, Microsoft wrote in the post. Citing CISA figures, the researchers said the mean time from CVE publication to listing in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. For 2026 through September, the mean has dropped to 20 days and the median to three. “Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure,” the post said. items.title: Hackers put porn on public billboards and claim it was “far too easy”
items.summary: A hacking group called Leakers$ gained access to remote management software for billboards and used it to show porn.
items.raw: While digital billboards are supposed to grab your attention, recent reports from Egypt , Malaysia, and Brazil described them doing so with explicit footage. The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays. The group said it did not hack into individual billboards to show the pornographic footage, but that it accessed the software used to send the content. For example, on October 29, explicit footage appeared on a large billboard overlooking one of Egypt’s busiest highways. Videos circulating online showed the attackers’ aliases and a Telegram channel address overlaid on the footage. Some motorists stopped to record it. Egyptian authorities said the billboard’s operator suffered a website compromise, resulting in unauthorized footage appearing in several countries simultaneously. Similar events were reported in Malaysia and Brazil. The attackers also claimed access to systems in Iraq and China, but those claims are less firmly corroborated. Speaking to The Cairo Report, a representative of Leakers$ claimed the group found thousands of exposed systems during roughly two hours of automated scanning. The representative described a vulnerability in content-transmission software and weaknesses accessible through the systems’ own web pages and interfaces. That is the group’s account, but if it is accurate, it helps explain the apparent ease and reach of the attack: Internet exposure makes targets discoverable. Attackers can scan for reachable management systems rather than physically approach individual screens. Repeated software weaknesses can scale. Finding a flaw in software used across multiple installations can create opportunities far beyond one billboard. Content-management access is the prize. Someone who gains control of the system that publishes advertisements may be able to replace legitimate content without touching the display itself. This is another example of how convenient remote management can expose systems to attack. Recent attacks on refrigerated systems in European supermarkets demonstrated a similar risk. The cooling systems are internet-connected, so mechanics can remotely diagnose and fix problems. items.raw: In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind , I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system. Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany: Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change. In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm. We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves. Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.

items.raw: Enterprises deploying large language models (LLMs) in production may be unknowingly footing the bill for someone else’s AI business. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) is warning of financially motivated LLMjacking campaigns in which cybercriminals hijack enterprise cloud and model access before reselling it through underground subscription services. The activity can generate fake cloud charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, GTIG said in a blog post . In some incidents, cumulative charges reached $1 million before organizations revoked the compromised access. “LLM Mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a service for paying customers, while the victim’s systems continue accepting requests through credentials they recognize,” said Piyush Sharma , co-founder and CEO at Tuskira. “That puts a lot of weight on the authority attached to each credential. A key issued for one application shouldn’t become a reusable pass to other models and workloads.” GTIG’s analysis is based on multiple incidents in 2026, spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. Stolen model access becomes an underground business GTIG said the monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, criminal routing gateways that aggregate compromised API credentials and resell model access to underground subscribers. These services proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption and hide the original source of access. Multiple operations were identified using open-source gateways and custom relay infrastructure to pool stolen credentials. One threat actor, UNC6993, used tools including new-api and gcli2api to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests across accounts. Another operation used stolen third-party API keys to power Jet Night, a legitimate token-routing service that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours, GTIG said. The activity passed nearly $1 million in token costs to the victim organization. Jet Night advertises unlimited access to frontier models for approximately $60 a month, substantially lower than the typical cost of comparable legitimate access. Jet Night also experienced occasional outages that GTIG suspects were caused by victims discovering compromises and revoking keys. “Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important,” said Ni

items.title: CISA’s new strategy runs into America’s blind trust problem
items.summary: Persistent credentials and forgotten software approvals leave essential operational networks vulnerable under CISA’s latest cybersecurity roadmap.
items.raw: An attacker with a working credential may find the system already open to them. That is the uncomfortable reality behind the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) new strategy , “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail.” The strategy prioritizes operational technology security, software supply chain integrity and continuity of essential services. It also acknowledges that strong defenses cannot guarantee that intrusions will stop. Federal agencies face these dependencies in building controls, research facilities and other operational systems. A compromised contractor credential or unverified update can turn an infrastructure problem into a mission disruption. How much infrastructure still trusts a device, software update or machine identity simply because it was approved once? Meeting CISA’s goals requires examining those approvals, including those no one remembers granting. Yesterday’s approval becomes today’s exposure A controller can stay in service for decades while its firmware, credentials, suppliers and connections change around it. A maintenance contractor leaves. A remote connection outlives its purpose. The hardware remains in place. The original reason for trusting it may no longer hold. An inventory is a starting point. Knowing a controller exists says little about whether its software is authentic, who can change its configuration or which systems depend on its credentials. Those questions cross organizational boundaries. Device security, software assurance and identity management may each have an owner. If every team owns one piece of trust, who owns the failure between them? CISA’s goals for operational technology visibility, anomaly detection and supply chain integrity should push operators to answer that question. Someone must be accountable for how devices, code and identities interact throughout their operational lives. That means verifying software before deployment, protecting signing keys and reassessing access when suppliers or roles change. Even then, authenticity has limits. A valid signature can confirm software origin and integrity. Whether the software is safe for a particular environment is a separate question. AI turns access into operational authority That distinction matters more when software can initiate action. Consider an AI agent evaluated for equipment diagnostics and maintenance. items.raw: A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps in their defenses before automated attacks exploit them. CrowdStrike reported that the group, tracked as VAPOR PANDA, used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17. The organizations included government agencies and businesses across at least 14 countries, with researchers confirming post-exploitation activity at nine. At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers instructed AI agents to examine running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to determine whether CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was installed, according to transcripts recovered by the cybersecurity firm. ARTEX uses multiple AI agents to carry out intrusion tasks under human direction. CrowdStrike found that VAPOR PANDA used the framework to pursue attacks against several organizations simultaneously, with operators intervening at key decision points. The findings follow an October 21 report from Microsoft detailing a separate campaign involving ARTEX. Microsoft said another China-linked group, Storm-0940 , used the framework to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours in some cases. The campaign included the abuse of compromised ConnectWise application credentials to access customer environments. Changing economics of cyberattacks The use of AI in cyberattacks is changing the economics of state-sponsored espionage by allowing smaller teams to pursue targets without a corresponding increase in personnel, according to Akshat Tyagi , associate practice leader at HFS Research. “The techniques are familiar, but the ability to run them in parallel is not,” Tyagi said. Jonathan Ong , senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia, said AI can substantially reduce the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, even as more sophisticated exploitation continues to require technical expertise. The attacks documented by CrowdStrike exploited weaknesses that security teams have encountered for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated. items.title: MLEP in KICS for Networks 5.0: how machine learning helps track network behavior of OT devices
items.summary: We explain how Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks uses Machine Learning Event Processor (MLEP) technology to help take inventory of assets and detect anomalies in industrial networks.
items.raw: In an industrial network, malicious activity can be hard to tell apart from normal data exchange between devices. Malicious actors routinely rely on legitimate tools and the Living-off-the-Land technique, so a single network connection may show no known signs of an attack: the device uses a familiar protocol and transmits ordinary data. An anomaly can hide in subtle details: the data source, the time of access, or the volume of transferred data may be atypical for a particular device. However, to detect this kind of anomaly, you need to understand the roles of the devices at both ends of the connection and know which network activity patterns are typical for them. But an organization’s asset inventory data is often incomplete, which makes it harder to catch unauthorized connections in time. Suppose monitoring detects a host that regularly exchanges data with programmable logic controllers (PLCs). Its IP address is known, but the inventory does not specify what role it plays: is it an engineering workstation, a process data server, or a piece of contractor’s equipment? The host may also have been on the industrial network for a long time, with its record going out of date after a network upgrade. In the joint OT asset inventory guidance released by CISA and its partners in 2025 , inventorying devices and classifying them by role are treated as part of OT asset management. For organizations, this is one of the most important areas: according to the SANS 2025 ICS security survey , 50% of respondents had deployed or significantly expanded ICS inventory and visibility tools over the previous 12 months, and 54% named them as investment priorities for the next 12–24 months. Device inventory in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks In Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks , the Asset Discovery technology is the foundation of asset visibility. Passive network traffic analysis detects devices and their interactions, while recognition rules help determine the device category and extract available information about it, such as the vendor, model, or software version. Exactly which attributes the system can obtain depends on the protocol and the traffic it observes. We covered this in more detail at the Kaspersky Industrial Cybersecurity Conference . items.summary: Google dismantled a 1.3 million-device botnet allegedly built by Android TV box maker Videostrong to enable ad fraud and proxy abuse. Google and its partners dismantled a backdoor called XCPE that had enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet. items.raw: Google dismantled a 1.3 million-device botnet allegedly built by Android TV box maker Videostrong to enable ad fraud and proxy abuse. Google and its partners dismantled a backdoor called XCPE that had enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet. The result of the investigation into the malware operation is the striking part: Videostrong Technology Co., an Android device maker, built and ran the botnet for money. Google says it is highly confident that Videostrong deliberately created, spread and operated the backdoor. The company reportedly sold access to criminal groups and installed their malware on infected devices. The malware was used for ad fraud, secretly added devices to residential proxy networks and installed other malicious software. Google says this was not the work of a rogue employee or a simple coding mistake. The backdoor was found in many device models and brands over several years. Its operation involved dedicated infrastructure and regularly changing configurations. “We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).” Google states . “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. “ Google has now cut all ties with Videostrong. The company is banned from making devices with pre-installed Google apps. The ban also covers any future subsidiaries or business partners, and Videostrong can no longer supply software to other certified device makers. Videostrong got around Google’s compatibility and security tests with code obfuscation. The malicious code loaded after a device’s first boot, which the tests didn’t catch. Google has changed its review process and is improving how it checks firmware on certified Android TV devices. Google also took legal action against the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet, and against the control domains of over a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Those affiliates spread their modules through other channels too, so Google expects the takedown to cut access to at least 10 million more compromised devices. items.raw: AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams. Security vendor Barracuda’s Cybersecurity Skills Gap report also found that security teams are struggling to keep pace with expanding responsibilities. The vast majority of the 2,000 IT and security decision-makers surveyed report cybersecurity skills gaps. In particular, the most common challenges are linked to AI-related risks (68%) and advanced identity and phishing threats (67%), including business email compromise , OAuth abuse, and multi-factor authentication bypass. Two-thirds (67%) of respondents say security teams are under pressure and struggling to scale to meet evolving business needs. Half say their security professionals are expected to support growing digital operations without additional resources. More than half (56%) report a reduction in security head count linked to AI, split evenly between entry-level and more senior roles. As AI takes on more routine analysis and response activities, human roles are shifting toward (higher value) threat investigation, incident leadership, automation governance, and business risk management. “AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than many security teams can build the necessary skills, visibility, and governance,” said Siroui Mushegian, senior vice president and chief information officer at Barracuda. “Organizations need to reshape their security teams, combining the power of AI and automation with human expertise, judgment, and visibility.” Hiring challenges CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that cloud security (35%), securing agentic AI technology (34%), and securing AI/machine learning-enabled technology (30%) topped the areas CSOs felt their teams needed to become more skilled and knowledgeable about in order to meet overall corporate security objectives. Underlining the difficulty of this ambition, the report found that cloud security architects, AI security specialist, and forensics analysts were the most difficult cybersecurity roles in which to find suitable applicants. Accessing the cost of the skills gap Separately, technology-focused online learning platform Pluralsight’s Tech Skills Report 2026 found that 41% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK estimate skills gaps cost them at least £380,000 each year (US$500,000). items.title: NIS2 Makes Board Members Personally Liable for Access Control Decisions
items.summary: NIS2 Article 20 makes management bodies answerable for the access controls they approve, and boards are starting to ask for proof that those controls work. NIS2 board accountability gives directors a more direct role in cybersecurity. Under Article 20, the management bodies of essential and important entities must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures required by […]
items.raw: NIS2 Article 20 makes management bodies answerable for the access controls they approve, and boards are starting to ask for proof that those controls work. NIS2 board accountability gives directors a more direct role in cybersecurity. Under Article 20, the management bodies of essential and important entities must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures required by the directive, oversee their implementation, and can be held liable for infringements, subject to national law. That obligation is live across most of the EU, with four member states going to the Court of Justice in July for failing to notify full transposition. Access control is one of the required measures. Directors are not expected to decide who gets administrator rights or review individual user accounts. They do, however, need to know that access is being controlled, that someone has responsibility for managing the risk, and that problems are being addressed. An estimated 160,000 entities fall within the scope of NIS2 across the EU. Approval is only part of the job Article 20 requires management bodies to both approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation. It also requires the members of those bodies to undergo cybersecurity training, and to offer comparable training to employees on a regular basis. The measures themselves are set out in Article 21. They include access control policies and asset management, along with the use of multi-factor authentication or continuous authentication solutions where appropriate. Many organizations have traditionally left these decisions to security and IT teams. Under NIS2, the board still needs to know whether the measures it approved are being implemented. Day-to-day responsibility can remain with the CISO and IT teams. The difficulty comes when the person responsible for a risk does not control the budget, systems, or people needed to address it. Greece’s implementation goes further in defining who carries that responsibility. Its NIS2 law requires essential and important entities to appoint a suitably qualified member of their organization as an Information and Communication Systems Security Officer. The officer coordinates compliance, must have the resources needed to do the job, and operates independently of the company’s data protection officer. items.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
items.summary: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
items.raw: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components). The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group. The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year , residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.” The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems . items.raw: Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday. The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults. In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution. The Monday attack, like the one in October, “resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers,” according to a Bloomberg report , which confirmed incidents with impacted retailers, including Carrefour, Spar, and Ahold Delhaize. No group has as yet claimed to be behind the attacks. A spokesman for Ahold Delhaize told CSO, “On Monday, November 2, we identified an incident affecting refrigeration systems in dozens of Delhaize stores. We immediately took the necessary measures to limit the impact and keep the stores operational.” The situation has since returned to normal, although the company had to discard valuable food, he said. Delay understandable Analysts and consultants said the lack of an immediate response to the initial refrigeration attacks is understandable, given the complex nature of the systems and the multiple vendors who typically manage such systems for major retailers. Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst Katell Thielemann said that although the impacted European retailers own the hardware, they outsource the maintenance, upkeep, and the management. Thus, she said, “there is some confusion about who owns what in this black box of outsourcing.” IDC Senior Research Manager Bobby Kuzma agreed. “There’s a huge gap in visibility between the folks who monitor threat intelligence and vulnerability reports, and the people who manage the OT/industrial side of the universe,” he said. “The cybersecurity teams may not have even been aware that the devices were network connected, especially if they were riding on dedicated internet circuits for manufacturer support.” Thielemann added that the incident was made worse because

items.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
items.summary: Your industrial IoT gateway isn't exposed to the internet, right? RIGHT?!
items.raw: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. items.title: Google shuts down global botnet running on certified Android devices
items.summary: Videostrong sold TV set-top boxes and other devices with pre-installed malware. The yearslong operation evaded Google’s security tests and established a botnet for cybercriminals.
items.raw: Google and an assortment of partners shut down a botnet that an approved Android device manufacturer purposefully deployed across more than 1.3 million TV set-top boxes, the company said Monday. Videostrong Technology Co., a China-based Android original equipment and device manufacturer, implanted a backdoor into multiple devices it sold. Those backdoors established XCPE, an expansive botnet that cybercriminals used to conduct ad fraud, steal data and route malicious traffic through residential proxy networks, according to a Google Threat Intelligence Group report. Google took legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet. The company also took down command-and-control domains that more than a dozen malware families ran as modules through the XCPE backdoor, claiming it disrupted access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices from various manufacturers. Videostrong sold Android devices with pre-installed malware for years, slipping by Google’s security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. “The XCPE operators constantly evolved its configurations to evade Google’s pre and post-launch detections,” Charley Snyder, head of disruption operations at GTIG, told CyberScoop. Snyder declined to say when or how Google first became aware of the approved vendor running a botnet on Android-powered devices. “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” Google researchers wrote in the report. “We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight.” Google banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries from building or selling certified Android devices, and said it changed its review process to detect and stop similar activities in the future. Yet, Snyder said the company isn’t sharing specifics on these changes because it doesn’t want to provide threat actors insights that might help them circumvent these additional protections. Most of the devices comprising the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes, but researchers also observed infected Android-based telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signs. “Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors,” researchers wrote in t

items.title: Business groups mount fresh campaign for long-term renewal of information sharing law
items.summary: Their target for extending CISA 2015 is the annual “must-pass” defense authorization bill, but a more than year-long standoff persists.
items.raw: Major industry groups are clamoring for Congress to include a 10-year extension of a law that they say is essential to cyber threat information sharing in the annual defense policy bill. Congress has mixed a series of short-term renewals and lapses of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 (CISA 2015) — which provides legal protections for threat data exchanges between the government and private sector as well as between companies — since its previous 10-year sunset came and went last year. It’s now set to expire again on Dec. 11 . On Sunday, 35 business groups sent a letter to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services panels, asking them to renew the law for 10 years as part of their final negotiations for the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. “The case for a long-term reauthorization has only grown more urgent,” they wrote. “Recent incidents have demonstrated that advanced AI systems can identify and exploit software vulnerabilities at machine speed, collapsing the window between the discovery of a weakness and its use in an attack.” “AI tools are also making sophisticated cyber capabilities cheaper, faster and easier to use, allowing threats to spread and adapt in real time,” they continued. “In this environment, the speed and breadth with which defenders share information determines whether they keep pace with adversaries. That speed depends on the legal certainty CISA 2015 provides.” The letter’s signatories include overarching business groups like the Chamber of Commerce and Business Roundtable, the latter of which led the letter, as well as groups representing critical infrastructure sectors such as aviation, telecommunications and technology. The House version of the fiscal 2027 defense bill includes a 10-year extension. The Senate version notably does not, and past efforts to include a long-term extension in the defense bill, which has been signed into law every year for decades, have encountered objections from Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky. Paul has hinged his support for any long-term extension of CISA 2015 on adoption of provisions designed to curtail past practices at the other CISA — the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency — that he maintains threaten free speech. items.title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
items.summary: Real-world exploitation concentrates in a small, high-impact subset of CVEs. Learn how defenders can prioritize vulnerabilities based on exploitation likelihood, exposure, and potential blast radius.
items.raw: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscape Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Impact, exposure and where to focus Next in line How Microsoft Security helps defenders act References Learn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification

items.title: Cops bust botnet of 1.3M infected Android TV boxes
items.summary: Videostrong accused of shipping devices with a backdoor baked in
items.raw: A coalition of private-sector security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. Google, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participated in the disruption. “We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology,” the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a Monday blog. Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. The firmware’s pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation. The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. “Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices,” according to GTIG. Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Videostrong did not immediately respond to The Register’s inquiries. This backdoor and botnet operation is part of the same ecosystem as BadBox 2.0, another notorious botnet that infected more than 10 million TV boxes and other devices before Human, Google, and TrendAI disrupted it in March 2025.®

items.title: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks
items.summary: As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM […]
items.raw: As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you. In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster. How DKIM replay works DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed. A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows: Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key. An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule. The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients. Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain. Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical. What an

items.title: Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool
items.summary: So, who's ready to clear the dust out of that server closet and move things back on-prem?
items.raw: If you're a customer of cloud-hosted AI workflow platform Trigger.dev, take heed, because your environment variables may have been exposed in a security incident disclosed on Sunday. Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an attacker had gained unauthorized access to environment variables belonging to those organizations. Whatever exploit was used to gain access has been blocked, the company added, and affected customers have been notified of steps they need to take to prevent further security problems. We likely don't have to tell The Reg readers how important environment variables are in SaaS and cloud services like Trigger. If compromised environment variables contain sensitive credentials, an attacker could basically end up with the keys to the kingdom, potentially gaining access to connected services and digital infrastructure. For those unfamiliar with Trigger.dev, it’s a platform for building AI agents and workflows in TypeScript, but here’s the kicker: Trigger advertises itself as a durable execution platform that handles pesky things like retries, scaling, and keeping long-running tasks going through crashes and redeployments, while providing tools to monitor what those tasks are doing. Trigger, the company’s site notes, can be used to “build durable AI agents that survive refreshes, redeploys, and crashes,” and is ideal for “long-running tasks with retries, queues, AI observability and elastic scaling.” In short, companies running their AI on Trigger probably want it to keep running, which makes stolen environment variables all the more dangerous. Elastic scaling, automated retries, and, as Trigger notes, the ability to run lots of concurrent operations without timeouts could compound the consequences of compromised API keys, depending on what those credentials allow an attacker to access. An attacker with stolen credentials could potentially interfere with a customer's connected services or workflows. Additionally, Trigger recently added webhooks to its offering, supporting services like Stripe, Supabase, and Slack, potentially expanding the range of integrations that could be affected if their credentials were exposed. This could be pretty bad for anyone affected. Trigger has some fairly high-profile customers, with companies like fashion brand Emporio Armani, Pentagon-supporting AI acquisitions platform GovSigna

items.title: Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges
items.summary: Don't let the LLMjackers hit you
items.raw: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register. “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking, and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Tele

items.raw: Overview INFINITT PACS installations using System Manager versions 3.0.11.3 and 3.0.11.5 contain vulnerabilities that may allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code. INFINITT Healthcare has remediated the issues in System Manager versions 3.0.12.3 and 3.0.12.5. Description INFINITT PACS is an enterprise web-based medical imaging platform that stores, retrieves, and displays patient scans. CVE-2026-16305 An improperly protected update manifest may allow a local attacker to execute commands with administrative privileges when an update is approved. SmartExecute.exe reads and runs commands from execlist.txt after an update. Because of insecure file permissions on execlist.txt , a low-privileged attacker can modify the file before it is processed to add arbitrary malicious commands. After SmartUpdate.exe launches, it runs SmartExecute.exe and the user can be prompted by User Account Control (UAC), which can allow the malicious command to execute with administrative privileges. CVE-2026-16306 An unsafe command dispatch through the registered imodular:// URI scheme may result in code execution. A vulnerability in IModular.exe allows an attacker to execute certain application functions by supplying a crafted imodular:// link. The application reads the cmd value from the link and executes the corresponding function without verifying that the command is permitted or safe. By convincing an end user to open a crafted imodular:// link, an attacker can cause IModular.exe to access attacker-controlled files or run specific programs from a local folder or network share. The link also accepts a url parameter that causes IModular.exe to connect to an attacker-controlled SignalR endpoint, creating an unauthorized outbound connection. Impact Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-16305 may allow a local, low-privileged attacker to execute arbitrary commands with administrative privileges on the affected workstation. An attacker could then install or modify software, access protected files, disable security controls, or establish persistent access to the system. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-16306 may allow a remote attacker to execute code with the privileges of the affected user, access or modify data available to that user, and use the compromised workstation as a foothold for further attacks. items.title: Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps
items.summary: Within minutes of a ceasefire lifting in Kherson, Ukraine’s citizens were pummelled with threatening notifications
items.raw: Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public. Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening. According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears. "The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices. "Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation." The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system. "Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government. According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards. Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine. items.title: 5 stars for sale: Inside the underground fake review trade
items.summary: Underground sellers offer five-star reviews and charge up to $1,100 to make negative feedback disappear.
items.raw: Recently, our team exposed sophisticated scam kits designed to steal sensitive data and trick consumers. But underground marketplaces are not just for malware and stolen passwords. They also offer services designed to manipulate your opinion of the products and services you buy every day. In our latest research, we examined cybercrime forums where sellers advertise illicit “reputation management” services. For the right price, these underground operators offer to flood a product with glowing, five-star ratings or remove negative reviews. This shadowy industry works both ways—artificially boosting reputations and deliberately hiding legitimate complaints. A major shift we are seeing in this space is the adoption of new technology. We also found that cybercriminals are using AI to automate these fake review campaigns. This could allow them to quickly generate realistic, human-sounding feedback in large volumes without much manual effort. 5 stars as a service In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star review generation and negative review removal services. The seller’s operations span widely used platforms, including Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and various mobile app stores. By simply asking prospective buyers, “Just tell me which platform reviews you need?” the seller presents reputation manipulation as something buyers can just order on demand. Five-star reviews and removal services Decoding the seller’s FAQ Analyzing another seller’s (TrustForge) “Frequently Asked Questions” section revealed some surprising details about how these operations reportedly run behind the scenes. First, the seller emphasizes that real people manually post these reviews, offering a guarantee for both successful delivery and “non-drop”—meaning the platform won’t flag and remove the feedback later. Remember, a real person posting a review doesn’t mean they’re a real customer. The important question is whether they actually used the product or service and are describing an honest experience. Second, it appears this is a well-coordinated team effort rather than a solo operation, as the seller charges an extra fee if a buyer wants the main operator to write the review text personally.
